text: The Microsoft AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO, also called DxO) is described in a paper titled 'Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models'. A preprint appeared on arXiv in 2025, and the peer-reviewed version was published in Science on Thursday, 22 October 2026.
topic: Microsoft's AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), which works through a case step by step like a doctor, was published in Science on 22 Oct 2026. Microsoft says

text: DxO works sequentially. It starts from a chief complaint and decides which follow-up questions and tests to order, instead of receiving a full patient file at once.
topic: Microsoft's AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), which works through a case step by step like a doctor, was published in Science on 22 Oct 2026. Microsoft says

text: The system simulates a panel of physicians. AI agents take roles such as proposing diagnoses, selecting tests, challenging assumptions and weighing costs. The authors suggest this may reduce cognitive biases such as anchoring.
topic: Microsoft's AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), which works through a case step by step like a doctor, was published in Science on 22 Oct 2026. Microsoft says

text: Gizmodo reports that on complex NEJM cases, DxO reached 83.2% accuracy. Generalist physicians with reference materials reached 36.1%.
topic: Microsoft's AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), which works through a case step by step like a doctor, was published in Science on 22 Oct 2026. Microsoft says

text: When generalist physicians were denied reference materials, their accuracy dropped to roughly 22%, which Gizmodo says makes DxO nearly four times as accurate.

text: On emergency department admissions, DxO scored 80.3% against 46.8% for generalists, a narrower margin.
